results.content:
What it does not provide is infrastructure built specifically for cold outreach. Infraforge fills that gap with dedicated IPs, automated DNS setup, sender rotation, intelligent sending limits, warm-up, and deliverability monitoring.

So the difference is clear. OpenMail is built around the agent's inbox. Infraforge is built around cold outreach infrastructure.

## What Are Users Saying About OpenMail?

Independent feedback on OpenMail is still very limited, which makes it difficult to judge the product from customer reviews alone.

On G2 and TrustPilot, OpenMail currently has zero reviews. Its profile explicitly says the product has not been reviewed yet, so there is no G2 feedback on reliability, deliverability, support, or day-to-day use. [...] SourceForge has one verified user review, giving OpenMail an overall 5/5 rating. The reviewer used it daily for less than six months and liked how it helped give an OpenClaw agent email access. They also rated support 5/5 and mentioned getting fast help through Discord. The main drawback was onboarding, which they found a little tricky because of the number of integrations available.

OpenMail user review on SourceForge

This image shows the OpenMail user review on SourceForge

There are also a few useful mentions on Reddit. One developer said OpenMail, AgentMail, and Hostinger Agentic Mail had been helpful for workflows because dedicated agent inboxes made them easier to manage.

Reddit discussion about Openmail

This image shows the Reddit discussion about Openmail [...] ‍
 The biggest drawback is the lack of independent feedback. OpenMail currently has no G2 reviews, making it difficult to assess its reliability, support, or real-world performance.  
  ‍
 My take: OpenMail is best suited to AI agents that need dedicated inboxes and two-way email conversations. If cold outreach infrastructure is your main priority, Infraforge is the more relevant alternative to consider.

results.content:
OpenMail is mainly for developers who need to give AI agents their own email inboxes.  
  ‍
 Each agent can send and receive emails, read full threads, handle attachments, and get new replies through webhooks or WebSockets.  
  ‍
 It can be used for support agents, sales agents, OTP verification, signup automation, and document processing.  
  ‍
 The free plan gives you 3 inboxes and 3,000 emails per month. Pro starts at €9 per month and adds 10 inboxes, custom domains, and 10,000 emails.  
  ‍
 Cold outreach is supported, but new inboxes have stricter cold sending limits during their first 30 days.  
  ‍
 Dedicated sending IPs are only available on the Enterprise plan.  
  ‍
 There are no OpenMail user reviews on G2 or Trustpilot yet.  
  ‍ [...] ‍
 OpenMail is mainly an email layer for AI agents, so you still need to build or connect the agent that decides what to send, how to handle replies, and what action to take next. [...] 1. Strict cold email limits cap new inboxes at 20 cold emails per day for their first 30 days. Account-level cold sending limits also apply.  
   ‍
2. Adding inboxes does not increase your cold email quota because OpenMail also applies a combined account-level cold sending limit.  
   ‍
3. No AI agent included means you still need to build or connect the agent that decides what to send and how to handle replies.  
   ‍
4. No built-in prospect database means OpenMail does not find the people or companies you want to contact.  
   ‍
5. Custom domains require a paid plan because Free accounts use OpenMail addresses, while custom domains are available on Pro and Enterprise.  
   ‍
6. Dedicated sending IPs require Enterprise while Free and Pro use shared sending IPs.

results.title: In-depth OpenMail Reviews - Features, Pricing & Alternatives
results.content:
### When to Look Elsewhere

OpenMail is not a great fit if you’re sending cold email at scale, because the rate limits get in the way before the pricing does.

 It’s also a poor fit for cold outreach teams, since the account cap is 500 sends a day.  
  ‍
 Agencies running client campaigns may find 200 sends a day per inbox too limiting.   
  ‍
 If you need reputation isolation, dedicated IPs are only on Enterprise.   
  ‍
 If Bcc matters, this isn’t the right product, since it’s blocked.   
  ‍
 If you want proof from other customers, there aren’t any public reviews.   
  ‍
 Finally, if you need a sequencer, OpenMail stops at the API.   
  ‍
 It’s also not the right choice if you need mail preserved after deletion, because deleting an inbox is permanent. [...] I have never struggled to send. Resend, SendGrid, and Postmark all handle that well. Receiving is where I end up writing IMAP polling loops, parsing MIME by hand, and stitching threads back together from headers.

OpenMail's pitch is that none of that should be my problem. One address per agent, replies delivered as structured JSON in under 500ms, attachments already parsed to text.

I found the docs unusually detailed, which is what made this review possible. They were also my only source, since nobody has publicly written about running this in production.

So I built this review on what OpenMail commits to in writing, and on the places where its own pages disagree with each other.

Table of Contents [...] ## TL;DR: OpenMail Review

 Built for agents, not campaigns: one inbox per agent, two-way threading, and no sequencer.  
  ‍
 Free tier needs no card: three inboxes, 3,000 emails, and omail.sh addresses only.  
  ‍
 Pro starts at €9/month: 10 inboxes are included, then it’s €1 per inbox with no cap.  
  ‍
 Replies arrive in under 500ms: delivered via WebSocket or webhook, with the full thread returned as JSON.  
  ‍
 Attachments come back as text: PDFs, images, Office files, and CSVs are parsed automatically.  
  ‍
 Key scoping is the standout: an inbox-scoped key can’t see its own rules.  
  ‍
 Cold sending is capped hard: 500 emails a day account-wide, and adding more inboxes doesn’t increase it.  
  ‍
 No public reviews exist: nothing on G2, Trustpilot, Reddit, or Hacker News.
